body.text: State vs. federal R&D tax credits: U.S. businesses claiming the federal IRC §41 research credit may also claim state credits, but most states count only in-state research and apply their own rates, bases, caps, deadlines and refund, transfer or carryforward rules. Because the §280C(c) election changes federal taxable income, many state returns are affected too.

Rates, thresholds and deadlines are stated as of the effective dates given. Where only practitioner commentary could be located, the text says so. Nothing in this report is legal or tax advice, and every figure should be confirmed against the current form instructions for the year being filed.
Summary

The federal credit for increasing research activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §41 sets the definitions that most state programs borrow, but the state credits differ from it in four ways that matter in practice. First, they count only research performed inside the state (and, in Colorado, only inside a designated enterprise zone). Second, they use their own rates and base calculations, sometimes with state-specific gross receipts. Third, they offer very different ways to monetize unused credit: cash refunds, sales or transfers, offsets against payroll withholding or other non-income taxes, or nothing beyond a carryforward. Fourth, many are subject to statewide caps, pre-certification and fixed application windows that the federal credit does not have. The federal side also interacts with the states through federal taxable income: the IRC §280C(c) choice between reducing the research deduction and electing a reduced credit changes the starting point that many state returns use.

The most consequential federal points remain: the regular-credit worked example must apply the 50% minimum base rule of §41(c)(2); and Form 6765 Section G was optional for tax year 2025 and is mandatory for most filers for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, which the IRS confirmed in the final Form 6765 instructions released in February 2026.
The Federal Credit: The Baseline States Build On
Origin and status

The credit was first enacted in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 as a temporary provision. Congress allowed it to lapse and extended it many times over the following three decades, often retroactively, until the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 (Division Q of Pub. L. 114-113) made it permanent effective from the 2015 tax year (Congressional Research Service, R48848; U.S. Treasury). Permanence matters for the state comparison because several states define their credits by cross-reference to §41 "as in effect" on a particular date, and others conform to the Internal Revenue Code on a rolling basis; the federal credit's permanence means those cross-references no longer risk pointing to an expired provision, although state conformity dates still determine which version of §41 and §174/§174A a state applies.
Qualified research and qualified research expenses

Under IRC §41(d)(1), research qualifies only if (1) the related expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under §174A (the cross-reference updated by Pub. L. 119-21), (2) the research is undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature, (3) the information is intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and (4) substantially all of the activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a purpose relating to function, performance, reliability or quality. Most state credits adopt the same test by reference, which is why the federal qualification analysis is normally the foundation of every state claim; the states then layer on geographic and, in some cases, industry restrictions.

Qualified research expenses (QREs) under §41(b) are in-house research expenses (wages for qualified services and supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, plus certain amounts paid for the right to use computers) and contract research expenses. Supplies exclude land, improvements to land and property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (§41(b)(2)(C)). Contract research expenses generally count at 65% of the amount paid to a person other than an employee (§41(b)(3)(A)), with higher percentages for payments to qualified research consortia (75%) and for certain energy research payments to eligible small businesses, universities and federal laboratories (100%).

Geographic scope is the first point of divergence from the states. Section 41(d)(4)(F) excludes research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico and any possession of the United States, so the federal credit is available for research performed anywhere in the U.S. State credits, by contrast, generally require the research to be performed within the state, and the taxpayer must therefore be able to locate each wage dollar, supply cost and contract payment geographically.
Regular Research Credit (RRC) versus Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC)

RRC. The regular credit equals 20% of the excess of QREs for the tax year over a base amount (§41(a)(1)), plus 20% of basic research payments and amounts paid to energy research consortia under §41(a)(2) and (3). The base amount is the fixed-base percentage multiplied by the average annual gross receipts for the four tax years preceding the credit year (§41(c)(1)); the fixed-base percentage may not exceed 16% (§41(c)(3)(C)); and the base amount may never be less than 50% of current-year QREs (§41(c)(2)). Start-up companies use special fixed-base percentage rules under §41(c)(3)(B).

body.text: The minimum base rule also matters for the states. Several state credits that are computed by reference to a federal-style base (for example, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Georgia and Indiana) inherit an analogous floor, so an overstated federal excess will usually overstate the state excess as well. Where a state uses its own gross receipts in the fixed-base calculation (Georgia and California are the clearest examples), the state base can differ materially from the federal base even when the QREs are identical.

ASC. The ASC equals 14% of the amount by which QREs exceed 50% of the average QREs for the three preceding tax years (§41(c)(4)(A)); if the taxpayer has no QREs in any one of those three years, the credit is 6% of current-year QREs (§41(c)(4)(B)).

Average QREs, prior three years

body.text: A growing number of states have adopted an ASC-style method of their own, which reduces the record-keeping burden of reconstructing historical gross receipts: Texas (from 2026, on a three-period average), California (from 2025, replacing its Alternative Incremental Credit), Indiana, Wisconsin, Delaware (as a share of the federal ASC) and Iowa's legacy credit (for 2025 and earlier). The federal election does not bind the state election in every state, so the method choice should be evaluated separately for each jurisdiction.

Amended-return ASC elections. T.D. 9666 (June 3, 2014) issued temporary and final regulations removing the prior bar in Treas. Reg. §1.41-9(b)(2) on electing the ASC on an amended return; T.D. 9712 (February 27, 2015) finalized the rule. The election is available on an amended return only if the taxpayer has not previously claimed the §41(a)(1) credit on an original or amended return for that year (including a return that showed zero), and only before the assessment period for that year closes. A member of a controlled group may not make the election on an amended return if any member previously claimed the regular credit for a tax year ending with or within the taxpayer's year. State amended-return rules are separate and frequently stricter; for example, application-based programs such as Florida's, Maryland's and Michigan's cannot be reopened by amending a return after the application or tentative-claim deadline has passed.

ASC 730 Directive. The IRS's Large Business and International (LB&I) Directive applies only to LB&I taxpayers, which the IRS defines as those with assets of $10,000,000 or more. Where its requirements are met (including U.S. GAAP certified audited financial statements that separately state R&D expense under ASC 730, and use of those statements for Schedule M-3), LB&I examiners accept adjusted financial-statement R&D as the starting point for QREs. A review or compilation report does not qualify. The directive has no state counterpart: state auditors are not bound by it, and the in-state sourcing of the financial-statement amounts must still be supported independently.

As a matter of statute, the fixed-base percentage for an established taxpayer is computed from tax years beginning after 1983 and before 1989 (§41(c)(3)(A)), which is the likely origin of the "1980s" description, and §41(f)(3) contains adjustment rules for acquisitions and dispositions that can make the regular-credit base difficult to reconstruct; neither provision compels an ASC election.
Monetizing the federal credit

Unused general business credits, including the research credit, carry back one year and forward 20 years (§39(a)(1)). A qualified small business (QSB) may elect to apply part of the credit against the employer share of social security tax and, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022, against the employer share of Medicare tax. Under §41(h)(3)(A) the taxpayer must have gross receipts of less than $5,000,000 for the tax year and no gross receipts for any tax year preceding the five-tax-year period ending with that year. The election limit is $250,000, increased by $250,000 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022, for a total of $500,000 (§41(h)(4)(B)(i)), and a taxpayer may make the election for no more than five tax years. The federal payroll offset has state analogues only in a few places (Georgia's withholding offset is the closest), so a start-up that relies on the federal payroll election should not assume a parallel state cash benefit.
Form 6765 Section G

In IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025) the IRS announced that Section G is optional for all filers for tax year 2025 (processing year 2026). The final instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), released February 6, 2026, confirm that Section G is optional for all taxpayers for the 2025 tax year and mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, with exceptions retained for certain filers, including QSBs electing the payroll tax offset and taxpayers below the instructions' size thresholds. The IRS also extended the 45-day period for perfecting a research credit refund claim through January 10, 2027 (practitioner summaries of the IRS announcement).
Where State Credits Diverge from the Federal Credit
Geographic nexus and apportionment

Because state credits count only in-state research, a multistate taxpayer cannot carry its federal QREs onto state returns. Wages, supplies and contract research have to be sourced to the state where the work was physically performed, and the base-period amounts must be sourced the same way. Several states go further and depart from federal definitions altogether. Colorado's enterprise zone credit, under C.R.S. §39-30-105.5, is 3% of the amount by which expenditures for research and experimental activities "in the enterprise zone" exceed the taxpayer's average of such expenditures in the same area for the two preceding income tax years; Colorado Department of Revenue guidance (FYI Income 22) measures those expenditures under the §174 definition rather than §41 and requires third-party research to be performed within the zone. Vermont and Nebraska take the opposite approach: they start from the federal credit itself and allow a percentage of the portion attributable to in-state research, which makes the federal computation the direct input to the state credit.

Sourcing rules also interact with remote work. Because state credits follow the location of the research activity, an employee working remotely from another state generally generates QREs for that other state, not for the employer's headquarters state. Taxpayers with distributed engineering teams therefore need time-and-location records at the employee level to support each state claim, a requirement the federal credit does not impose.
Refundability, transferability and carryforwards
The federal credit is nonrefundable apart from the QSB payroll offset and carries forward 20 years. State treatment varies widely.

Delaware (approved credit exceeding liability is paid as a refund); Nebraska; Hawaii (qualified high technology businesses, subject to a $5 million statewide cap); Michigan (new for 2025, subject to a $100 million aggregate cap with proration); Iowa (the new IEDA-administered program from 2026 is capped at $40 million per year, with refundability phasing down according to practitioner sources)

Wisconsin (up to 25% for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2024); Minnesota (19.2% for 2025, 25% for 2026 and 2027); Texas (from January 1, 2026, for entities owing no franchise tax); Maryland (small-business credits); New Mexico (additional credit for qualified small businesses). Virginia's refundable standard credit is no longer available for new expenses: it applied only to taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025.

Saleable or transferable

Pennsylvania (sale or assignment with DCED approval); Missouri; Arkansas (targeted-business credits); North Dakota (qualifying primary sector businesses); New Jersey (through the NJEDA Technology Business Tax Certificate Transfer Program; practitioner sources only); Connecticut (exchange with the state for a 65% refund by qualified small businesses)

body.text: IRC §174/§174A and the §280C(c) election: the federal-to-state link

Current law. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, enacted July 4, 2025) added §174A, which allows an immediate deduction for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, with an election to capitalize and amortize over not less than 60 months instead. Transition rules permit certain small businesses (average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less) to apply §174A retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, and permit any taxpayer to deduct unamortized domestic amounts from 2022 through 2024 either in the first tax year beginning after December 31, 2024 or ratably over two years. Foreign research expenditures remain capitalized and amortized over 15 years under amended §174(a).

State conformity to §174A is not uniform. States that conform to the Internal Revenue Code on a rolling basis generally pick up §174A automatically, while fixed-date conformity states must enact legislation to adopt it, and some states decoupled from the 2022–2024 amortization regime or from the new expensing rules. Michigan, for example, considered and rejected full conformity on revenue grounds in connection with its new credit (practitioner reports of Treasury's revenue estimate). Because the state research deduction and the state credit are computed separately, a taxpayer can face immediate expensing federally and capitalization in a decoupled state for the same expenditures; the state credit QREs, however, are unaffected by that difference.

§280C(c). As amended by Pub. L. 119-21 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, §280C(c)(1) reduces the domestic research or experimental expenditures otherwise taken into account under §174A (whether deducted or charged to capital account) by the amount of the §41(a) credit. A taxpayer may instead elect a reduced credit equal to the credit determined under §41(a) minus the product of that credit and the maximum rate of tax under §11(b) (currently 21%). The election must be made on a timely filed original return, including extensions, and once made is irrevocable for that year. In the current codified text, the reduced-credit election appears at §280C(c)(2). Practitioner literature still commonly uses the older "(c)(3)" label from the pre-2025 version of the section.

Deduction reduced by $100,000, so federal taxable income rises by $100,000
Reduced-credit election
No reduction to the deduction

body.text: State consequence. Many states begin their corporate income tax computation with federal taxable income. Without the election, the higher federal taxable income carries into those states' starting points; with it, the starting point is unaffected by the credit (KBKG commentary; specific state conformity rules were not verified state by state). Some states require their own addback or permit their own subtraction for the §280C(c) adjustment, and a few states that conform to an earlier version of the Code will apply the pre-2025 text of §280C(c). Analysis: the right choice depends on the taxpayer's federal rate position, its state apportionment factors and how each state of filing conforms. Because the election is irrevocable and must be made on a timely original return, the state modeling must be completed before the federal return is filed.
How many states offer a credit?

Counts in the sources consulted range from more than 35 to 38, and the number has moved during 2025 and 2026: Michigan reinstated a credit for 2025, Virginia's credits ended for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, and Iowa replaced its entitlement credit with an application-based program from 2026. The Tax Foundation reports that 37 of the 47 states with corporate income taxes offer R&D incentives. No official count from a government source was located.

SB 2206 (signed June 17, 2025) replaced the former franchise tax credit and repealed the §151.3182 sales and use tax exemption effective January 1, 2026. The new credit is 8.722% of QREs above 50% of the three-period average (10.903% with a contract with a Texas institution of higher education), or 4.361% / 5.451% of current QREs where there were no QREs in any of the prior three periods. The pre-2026 franchise tax credit was 5% (6.25% with a higher-education contract), with an alternative computation where no prior-period QREs existed. The new credit conforms to federal §41 definitions as of a fixed date (practitioner sources).

Limited to 50% of franchise tax due; unused credit carries forward 20 consecutive reports; refundable for entities owing no tax under the no-tax-due or veteran-owned business exemptions. The former "either credit or sales tax exemption" choice no longer applies to periods after 2025.

10% of Florida QREs above the base; available only to C corporations that are qualified target industry businesses, certified by FloridaCommerce

The statewide cap under §220.196(2)(e), F.S., remains $9 million per calendar year (not $16.5 million, which applied only to 2018). body.text: What the Differences Mean (Analysis)
This section is interpretation, not a statement of law.

The federal calculation does not carry over to the states. Even states that adopt §41 definitions use their own rates, bases and sometimes their own gross receipts (California, Georgia) or their own expenditure definition (Colorado, which measures expenditures under §174 within an enterprise zone). A multistate claimant therefore needs separate in-state QRE and base histories for each state, maintained over at least the look-back period each state uses: two years for Colorado, three years for the ASC-style methods in Texas, California, Indiana and Wisconsin, and four years of gross receipts where a state follows the federal regular-credit structure. The federal Section G business-component detail, now mandatory for most filers for tax years beginning after 2025, is the natural foundation for those state histories, but only if it is captured with location data at the time it is prepared.

Monetization differs more than rates do. A 5% refundable or saleable credit can be worth more to a loss company than a higher nonrefundable rate with a 5-year carryforward. Recent changes moved in both directions. Texas, Michigan, Minnesota and Wisconsin added or expanded refundability. Georgia shortened its carryforward, California temporarily capped credit use at $5 million per year, Iowa replaced an entitlement credit with a capped discretionary award, and Virginia's refundable small-business credit expired with taxable years beginning in 2024. For an early-stage company, the existence of a refund, sale or payroll-offset route is usually the deciding factor; for a profitable multistate company, the interaction between rate, base and the state's limitation on the percentage of tax the credit may offset (50% in Georgia, South Carolina, Rhode Island and Texas; 75% in Massachusetts and for Virginia's legacy major credit) tends to matter more.

Caps and deadlines create timing risk the federal credit does not have. Florida, Hawaii, Maryland, Michigan, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Louisiana and the new Iowa program all ration credits through caps, windows or pre-certification. Missing a window (for example, Florida's March 20 to 26 period or Michigan's tentative-claim date) can forfeit a state credit even when the federal credit is secure. Caps also mean the value of an approved credit is uncertain until the agency publishes its allocation: Florida's $9 million cap, which the 2026 Legislature declined to raise, has historically produced heavy proration, and Michigan's first proration notice was published in April 2026, after many taxpayers' federal extended-return planning had begun. Taxpayers should treat capped state credits as contingent until the allocation notice is issued.

The §280C(c) decision is a state decision too. Because it changes federal taxable income, the election should be modeled across all states of filing before the original return is filed. The modeling should account for each state's conformity date (which determines whether the state applies the post-2024 text of §280C(c) and §174A), any state addback or subtraction for the §280C(c) adjustment, and the taxpayer's apportionment percentage in each state. A small federal saving from the reduced-credit election can be outweighed, or amplified, by the state effect.

Rules are changing year to year. At least ten of the programs changed between 2024 and 2026 (Texas, Iowa, California, Georgia, Minnesota, Michigan, Wisconsin, Virginia, Louisiana and, through the expiry of its legislation, the status quo in Florida), which is why this report states an effective date for each figure. The changes cluster around three themes: replacing older incremental computations with ASC-style methods (Texas, California), converting entitlement credits into capped, application-based programs (Iowa, Louisiana's new aggregate cap), and adding refundability to compete for early-stage research activity (Michigan, Minnesota, Texas). A taxpayer that last reviewed its state credit positions before 2025 should assume that at least one of its states of filing has changed its rules.
